av_event.line_text: That's a blessing, being close. Really. Look after him. You only get them once.
av_event.what: Before speaking, Abdul goes quiet for about three seconds and looks down and away from the screen. His broad smile drops, he presses his lips together, then looks back up at the camera and speaks more softly than before.

text:
B: Hello, hello! Can you hear me okay?
A: Yeah, I can hear you fine. Hi.
B: Good, good. I'm Abdul. How are you doing today?
A: Not bad, thanks. Bit knackered, to be honest. I was on a late last night, so, erm, yeah. You?
B: Late shift? Yeah, me also, yesterday! I'm a porter at the hospital in Whitechapel, and the lifts in the old block broke down again, so I'm pushing the beds round the long way, you know, half the building. My legs are telling me about it today.
A: Oh no. That sounds rough.
B: It's okay, it's the job, innit. Sixteen years I'm doing it. What about you, what you do?
A: Erm, I work in a factory, chilled food, in Park Royal. I run a tray-sealing machine on the packing line. Ready meals, that sort of thing.
B: Ah, so the ones in the supermarket, the little trays with the film on top?
A: Yeah, that's us. Well, some of them. I've been there eleven years now, so I sort of... I train the new starters on the sealer as well, when they come in.
B: Eleven years, that's good, that's loyal. Same as me, they give me the new porters to show around, because I know every corridor. You must be patient, yeah? To train people.
A: I try to be. Erm, when I started someone was a bit sharp with me, and I remember how that felt, so I just take it slow with them, you know. Nobody learns anything if they're scared of the machine.
B: Exactly, exactly. Same with patients. Old lady, she's frightened going down to the scan, I just keep talking, talking, about the weather, cricket, anything. By the time we get there she's forgot she was worried.
A: That's nice, actually. I reckon the nurses must like you.
B: They ask for me by name sometimes! Makes me feel very important. Do you follow cricket at all?
A: Yeah, more than football really. I listen to the Tests on the radio app on my break. Though England... another collapse, wasn't it.
B: Don't talk to me about collapse! Bangladesh, last week, I was sure, sure they're going to win. I told my friends, I said relax, this one is easy. Then three wickets in two overs. Finished.
A: Oh, I saw that. That was painful.
B: Painful, yes. I used to play, Sunday tape-ball in Victoria Park, but my knees, after forty-five, they said no more, Abdul. Now I just umpire. Shout at everybody instead.
A: Ha. I play five-a-side with my cousins every couple of weeks, but they stick me in goal, so I don't have to run much.
B: Smart man! Goalkeeper is the best job. And the puzzle at the start, how did you find it? I was stuck on the third one a long time.
A: Erm, the one with the shapes? Yeah, I didn't finish it, to be honest. I sort of guessed the last two.
B: Me too, guessing! I put my glasses on, I thought they would help, but no.
A: Ha, yeah. Do you get many days off, with the rota?
B: Not so many. I am saving my leave, I go back to Sylhet every two, three years, so I take one month together. You have family round you?
A: Yeah, my parents are in Kenton, ten minutes away. My mum keeps sending food round, which, erm, I'm not complaining about. My dad's... he's slowing down a bit lately, so it's good being close, you know.
B: That's a blessing, being close. Really. Look after him. You only get them once.
A: Yeah. I try.
B: You're a good son, I can tell. So do you cover shifts, at your place, when they ask?
A: Erm, more than I should, probably. I find it hard to say no, sort of, and then I'm—
